scenarios.name: Complete melt of present-day land-ice inventory

time_reference.label: Present-day inventory described by source; hypothetical complete melt, not a dated forecast

scenarios.mechanism: Gravitationally grounded glaciers, ice caps and ice sheets add water to the ocean upon complete melting. Floating sea ice and floating ice shelves are not counted as equivalent grounded land-ice volume.

estimate.reference: Approximate global mean sea-level equivalent of the present-day glacier and ice-cap inventory; not relative local sea level.
estimate.confidence: Approximate; USGS notes uncertainty in total glacier and ice-cap volume.

source_references.title: How would sea level change if all glaciers melted?

limitations: This is not a plausible near-term forecast or a +200 m mechanism.
A global mean equivalent does not give local shoreline change; gravitational, rotational, ocean-dynamic and vertical-land-motion fingerprints matter.
Do not add floating sea-ice area as if it were grounded land ice.
scenarios.claim_ceiling: Approximate global water-equivalent reference only; no local inundation or timing claim.

scenarios.name: IPCC AR6 very-high-emissions likely range to 2100
scenarios.mechanism: Combined thermal expansion, land-ice mass loss and other assessed contributors under SSP5-8.5.

estimate.reference: Global mean sea level relative to 1995–2014.
estimate.confidence: Medium confidence; 17th–83rd percentile likely range in IPCC AR6.

scenarios.model_family: IPCC AR6 assessed global mean sea-level projection, SSP5-8.5

source_references.title: Climate Change 2021: The Physical Science Basis — Summary for Policymakers

limitations: Global mean projection, not a site-level relative sea-level projection.
Likely range does not include all low-confidence ice-sheet instability outcomes.
Scenario is conditional on an emissions pathway, not a probability forecast that SSP5-8.5 will occur.
scenarios.claim_ceiling: IPCC assessed global mean likely range; local adaptation requires regional sea-level and land-motion evidence.

scenarios.name: IPCC AR6 low-likelihood high-impact sea-level outcome beyond 2300
scenarios.mechanism: Very high greenhouse-gas emissions with deeply uncertain long-term ice-sheet instability and commitment processes.

estimate.reference: Global mean sea-level change relative to 1900; lower bound only, not a central estimate.
estimate.confidence: Low confidence; low-likelihood/high-impact outcome cannot be excluded.

scenarios.model_family: IPCC AR6 low-confidence long-term high-impact sea-level outcome

source_references.title: IPCC AR6 Synthesis Report Longer Report, Figure 3.4
source_references.source_role: Long-term high-impact sea-level framing and figure reference.

limitations: Not a likely range, median, or date-specific deterministic forecast.
Low confidence and deep uncertainty must remain visible.
Not a +200 m projection.
scenarios.claim_ceiling: Low-confidence high-impact stress boundary only; not a central planning forecast.

scenarios.name: Phanerozoic paleogeographic-flooding reconstruction peak

time_reference.label: Approximate peak near 80 Ma in the cited reconstruction

scenarios.mechanism: Reconstructed geological sea-level highstand shaped by changing ocean-basin capacity, tectonic evolution and long-term Earth-system processes; not equivalent to melting modern ice.

estimate.reference: Approximate reconstructed peak relative to present-day level as reported by the study.
estimate.confidence: Published reconstruction; highly method-dependent and contested by alternative long-term curves.

scenarios.model_family: Global Phanerozoic sea levels from paleogeographic flooding maps (2022)

source_references.title: Global Phanerozoic sea levels from paleogeographic flooding maps

limitations: Model output depends on palaeogeographic reconstructions, paleotopography and the flooding method.
A modern digital elevation model raised by 280 m is not a valid reproduction of the past geography.
Do not treat this single curve as consensus or independent of its underlying reconstructions.
scenarios.claim_ceiling: One published reconstruction hypothesis; use original palaeogeography and uncertainty, not a modern bathtub map.

scenarios.name: Long-term Phanerozoic strontium-isotope and glaciation reconstruction

time_reference.label: Cretaceous highstands; study reports peak estimates including approximately 117 Ma and 91 Ma

scenarios.mechanism: Tectono-glacio-eustatic reconstruction combining strontium-isotope variation and estimates of continental glaciation.

estimate.reference: Reported Cretaceous highstand estimates relative to present-day level in the study, including peak values at different geological ages.
estimate.confidence: Published reconstruction range; not a statistical confidence interval shared by all studies.

scenarios.model_family: Long-term Phanerozoic global mean sea level from strontium isotope variations and continental-glaciation estimates (2022)

source_references.title: Long-term Phanerozoic global mean sea level: Insights from strontium isotope variations and estimates of continental glaciation

limitations: The study reports Cretaceous highstands at different ages; do not label the entire 174–217 m range as Late Cretaceous.
Range is a study-reported reconstruction range, not a statistical confidence interval shared by all studies.
Tectonic, basin-volume and glaciation assumptions require independent review.
scenarios.claim_ceiling: Published reconstruction range only; retain source model and age semantics.

scenarios.name: Alternative Cenozoic sea-level reconstruction review

time_reference.label: Late Cretaceous peak as reconstructed by the 2026 review

scenarios.mechanism: Alternative sequence-stratigraphic and sedimentary-facies reconstruction challenging higher Late Cretaceous highstand estimates.

estimate.reference: Reported Late Cretaceous peak relative to present-day level in the 2026 review.
estimate.confidence: Recent published alternative reconstruction; should be evaluated against primary stratigraphic evidence and other model families.

scenarios.model_family: Persistent Cenozoic sea-level rise: historical evidence from sequence-stratigraphic and sedimentary facies studies in continental margin basins (2026)

source_references.title: Persistent Cenozoic sea-level rise: Historical evidence from sequence-stratigraphic and sedimentary facies studies in continental margin basins

limitations: This is an alternative reconstruction, not an agreed replacement for the 2022 curves.
The estimate should be rechecked against the full paper, data and subsequent critique before quantitative use.
Do not average conflicting reconstructions without a defensible model-combination method.
scenarios.claim_ceiling: Competing published reconstruction hypothesis; no consensus claim.

scenarios.name: Modern-terrain +200 m synthetic inundation stress test

time_reference.label: No geological time; imposed water-surface offset over a declared modern terrain model

scenarios.mechanism: An artificial uniform +200 m surface offset used to test data pipelines, network topology failure, and adaptation search behavior. No physical Earth process is asserted.

estimate.reference: Offset relative to the chosen modern terrain model vertical datum; not a global eustatic or local relative sea-level prediction.
estimate.confidence: Deterministic user-defined stress parameter; not an empirical estimate.

scenarios.model_family: Synthetic modern-surface offset; terrain and vertical datum must be pinned by each run

source_references.title: DEEP-TIME-INFRASTRUCTURE-001 scenario policy
source_references.source_role: Defines the synthetic-only claim ceiling and separation from physical projections.

limitations: Not a sea-level forecast, climate scenario, ice-melt outcome or Cretaceous paleogeography.
A modern bathtub overlay omits tectonics, dynamic topography, ocean-basin change, erosion, sedimentation, isostasy and evolving drainage.
Only supports software robustness and explicitly synthetic stress testing.
scenarios.claim_ceiling: Synthetic stress test only; must be visibly labelled and must not be presented as a physical Earth forecast.

scenarios.name: Next-supercontinent alternative future climate boundary conditions

time_reference.label: Two alternative Earth configurations modelled 200 and 250 million years into the future

scenarios.mechanism: Alternative plate-tectonic configurations, continental topography, ocean gateways, solar insolation and rotation-rate assumptions create materially different future climate boundary conditions.

estimate.reference: No sea-level offset is specified by this scenario record.
estimate.confidence: Comparative Earth-system modelling; not a prediction of city locations, coastlines or future sea-level height.

scenarios.model_family: The Climates of Earth's Next Supercontinent: Effects of Tectonics, Rotation Rate, and Insolation (2021)

source_references.title: The Climates of Earth's Next Supercontinent: Effects of Tectonics, Rotation Rate, and Insolation
source_references.source_role: Two alternative 200 and 250 Ma climate boundary-condition experiments.

limitations: The study compares alternative boundary conditions, not a precise prediction of one future supercontinent.
No city, canal alignment or engineering asset can be projected with present-day precision at this horizon.
Solar, tectonic, atmospheric and ocean assumptions must be revisited for any new model run.
scenarios.claim_ceiling: Comparative boundary-condition research only; no local infrastructure or sea-level forecast.
